Guided Inquiry

1 · The setup

A conducting rod sits on two rails inside a uniform magnetic field B (dots = out of the page). A resistor R closes the circuit at the left end. The field is constant — it never changes.

The rod is already sliding right at speed v. Notice the green shaded area it sweeps out — that is what changes.

2 · Predict — what happens to the opposing force?

Once current flows, the field pushes back on the rod with a retarding force. Suppose right now that force is F.

If you DOUBLE the rod's speed v, the opposing force becomes:

3 · Predict — and what about doubling B?

Same question, but now for the field.

If you DOUBLE the field B, the opposing force becomes:

4 · Observe — try both

The red arrow on the rod is the retarding force. The two bars beneath the rails are the power ledger — mechanical power in (F·v) against electrical power out (ε·I), both on a fixed 0.40 W scale.

• Double v: the arrow lengthens ×2, and both bars ×4 — power carries a second factor of v.
• Double B: the arrow lengthens ×4, and both bars ×4.
• At every setting the two bars stay the same length. That equality is the whole point.

5 · “Isn't the current free?”

Some students say: “The rod just glides, and current appears — that's free energy.” It isn't.

The moment current I flows through the rod, the field exerts F = BIL against the motion (Lenz). Keeping the rod moving costs F·v of mechanical power — exactly the ε·I dissipated in the resistor. No surplus, no deficit.

The field never changes. What changes is the circuit's area. Same law as Faraday's, seen from the other side.

The Physics

Motional EMF — Electricity Costs You a Push · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A metal rod slides along two rails in a steady magnetic field, and a resistor closes the circuit at one end. The sim follows what happens in the circuit and in the rod as you change the speed, the field and the resistance.

What you'll learn

  • How the EMF, the current and the force on the rod are linked in this circuit.
  • How the power you put in compares with the power the circuit gives out.
  • What changes in the circuit even though the field itself never changes.
A rod on two rails, joined by a resistor R. The rails are a distance L apart and the rod moves with speed v.

What's on screen

  • Rod and rails: the amber rod with a cyan arrow for its speed v, the rails, the resistor at the left, and the field dots.
  • Green strip: the area the rod has swept since the run began. Teal arrows show the current I.
  • Red arrow: the retarding force F on the rod.
  • Live readouts in the side panel: ε, I, F and two powers. Two power bars sit under the rails.
See itRun the opening setting: v = 3 m/s, B = 0.50 T, R = 2.0 Ω. Watch for: the rod sliding right and the green strip growing behind it.

03

A moving rod makes an EMF in the loop

The rod, the two rails and the resistor form a closed loop. When the rod moves at speed v, the loop's area grows by L·v every second. The field B points straight through the loop, so the flux Φ = B × (area) grows at the rate B L v. Faraday's law turns that rate into an EMF:

ε = B L v
B in tesla, L in metres, v in m/s gives ε in volts.

The field never changes. The flux changes because the loop's area does, and the green strip shows that area. At the opening values ε = 0.50 × 0.20 × 3.0 = 0.30 V.

Lenz's law gives the direction. The current must oppose the growth of the outward flux, so it circulates clockwise: down the rod, along the bottom rail, up through R and back along the top rail.

See itSet v = 6 m/s, with B = 0.50 T and R = 2.0 Ω. Watch for: the readout ε = 0.60 V, and the green strip growing at twice the rate of the opening run.
04

The current brings a force on the rod

The EMF drives a current through the resistor, and the same current runs through the rod:

I = ε / R = B L v / R
Opening values: 0.30 V / 2.0 Ω = 0.150 A.

A rod of length L carrying current I in a field B feels a force F = B I L. By Lenz's law it opposes the rod's motion, so it points left while the rod moves right. Putting the two results together:

F = B I L = B² L² v / R
Opening values: 0.50 × 0.150 × 0.20 = 0.0150 N.

The sim holds v constant, as if something pushes the rod forward with exactly this force.

See itRun the opening setting and read the three readouts. Watch for: ε = 0.30 V, I = 0.150 A and F = 0.0150 N, with the red arrow pointing left from the rod.
05

The force depends on v and B differently

In F = B² L² v / R the speed v appears once, through the EMF. The field B appears twice: once in the EMF, and again in the force law F = B I L. So changing v and changing B do not have the same effect on F. Starting from the opening values:

ChangeFCompared with 0.0150 N
v from 3 to 6 m/s0.0300 N2×
B from 0.50 to 1.0 T0.0600 N4×

The red arrow is drawn in proportion to F, so these ratios show directly in its length. If the arrow would run into the resistor, the sim cuts it off and marks it as clipped.

See itRaise B to 1.0 T with v = 3 m/s and R = 2.0 Ω. Watch for: F = 0.0600 N, and the red arrow 4 times as long as in the opening run.
06

Resistance sets the current, not the EMF

The formula ε = B L v has no R in it, so the resistor never changes the EMF. It decides how much current that EMF can drive, and so how hard the field pushes back. With v = 3 m/s and B = 0.50 T, ε stays at 0.30 V:

RI = ε / RF = B I L
0.5 Ω0.600 A0.0600 N
2.0 Ω0.150 A0.0150 N
10 Ω0.030 A0.0030 N

A smaller R draws more current and so exerts a bigger force on the rod. A very large R draws almost no current and almost no force, yet the rod still has an EMF between its ends.

See itLower R to 0.5 Ω with v = 3 m/s and B = 0.50 T. Watch for: ε still 0.30 V, while I rises to 0.600 A and F to 0.0600 N.
07

The push is paid for in power

Moving the rod at speed v against a force F takes mechanical power P = F v. In the circuit, the EMF drives current I, so the resistor receives electrical power ε I, which it turns into heat. Both come out the same:

F v = B² L² v² / R = ε I
Opening values: 0.0150 × 3.0 = 0.30 × 0.150 = 0.0450 W.

If a current flowed with no force on the rod, the circuit would give out power with nothing supplying it. The force is what makes the books balance: the energy dissipated in R is the work done by whoever pushes the rod. The two bars under the rails use one fixed scale of 0.40 W, so their lengths compare directly. Power goes as v², once from F and once from the factor v.

See itRaise v to 6 m/s, with B = 0.50 T and R = 2.0 Ω. Watch for: the two bars equal in length at 0.1800 W each, 4 times the opening 0.0450 W.
08

Where it matters

  • Generators. A generator's coil moves through a magnetic field, so an EMF is induced. The turbine must supply the torque that works against the retarding force of this sim, and that force grows as more current is drawn.
  • Regenerative braking. In an electric car or train the motor can run as a generator while slowing down. The braking force is this force, and the energy goes back to the battery instead of being lost as heat in the brake pads.
  • Eddy-current brakes. A metal plate moving through a magnetic field has currents induced in it, and the field pushes back on them. This slows roller-coaster cars and heavy trains without any contact.
09

Summary

In one line. In a rod-on-rails circuit, the EMF, the current, the force on the rod and the power all follow from B, L, v and R.

Key points

  • ε = B L v, and I = ε / R.
  • F = B I L = B² L² v / R, opposing the motion by Lenz's law.
  • Mechanical power F v equals electrical power ε I.

Common mix-ups

  • "The current is free energy." The current brings a force that opposes the motion, so keeping the rod moving costs exactly the power the resistor dissipates.
  • "The field changes, so an EMF appears." The field is constant here. The flux changes because the loop's area changes.
  • "Doubling B doubles the force." B appears in both ε and F = B I L, so the force goes up by 4×.

Things to try on your own

  • Set v = 4 m/s and work out F and P by hand before you read them from the panel.
  • With B = 1.0 T and v = 3 m/s, find the resistance that gives the same force as the opening setting. One answer is R = 8 Ω.
  • Set R = 10 Ω and compare ε with its opening value, then I.
